Neurology · published research

Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)

In mice, 830-nm PBM during the acute phase reduced edema and thermal hypersensitivity in selected protocols, while mechanical hypersensitivity did not differ significantly overall. The six-person human CRPS subgroup report found no statistically significant group-level pain or autonomic improvement.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In mice, 830-nm PBM during the acute phase reduced edema and thermal hypersensitivity in selected protocols, while mechanical hypersensitivity did not differ significantly overall. The six-person human CRPS subgroup report found no statistically significant group-level pain or autonomic improvement.

Summary of the Evidence

The direct CRPS category contains one mouse publication. A narrow adjacent-category mapping adds one nicotine-associated CRPS-I mouse study and one older human report on stellate-ganglion irradiation. These three titles are different evidence types, not three clinical studies. The human report included only six people with CRPS in its blinded second phase; it also enrolled healthy controls and used a broad polarized-light treatment rather than a standard PBM device.

Human and clinical evidence

Basford et al. studied polarized light spanning 0.6–1.6 μm at the stellate ganglion. Three of six participants with CRPS reported warmth and two reported more than 50% pain reduction, but the group-level pain change was not statistically significant and autonomic measures did not change significantly (Basford et al. 2003). This small report does not provide a reliable estimate of clinical efficacy. No adequately powered trial of a defined PBM protocol for CRPS was identified.

Animal evidence

In a randomized mouse model, 830-nm PBM applied to the affected paw during the acute phase reduced edema and thermal hypersensitivity in selected groups. Mechanical hypersensitivity did not differ significantly between groups overall (Canever et al. 2021). A second mouse study induced CRPS-like changes with nicotine and found reductions in thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity with 660- or 830-nm treatment, with stronger effects reported for 660 nm (Rodrigues et al. 2020). These are model-specific outcomes.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo CRPS study was identified. Tissue and inflammatory measurements were part of animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The mouse studies used localized red or near-infrared light at 660, 830 nm or both, applied to the paw or a related spinal region. The older human report used linearly polarized red and near-infrared light delivered transcutaneously over the stellate ganglion, with 0.92 W output and 88.3 J total energy reported. That broad-spectrum exposure and anatomical target differ from the mouse PBM protocols and from routine rehabilitation treatment.

Interpretation

The evidence supports a testable analgesic and edema-reduction effect in mouse CRPS models. It does not establish that PBM improves pain, limb use or autonomic symptoms in patients. The only mapped human observation is too small and technically different to resolve that question.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for human pain or function outcomes Low for selected edema and thermal-sensitivity outcomes in mouse models
Publications and records3 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The human report used polarized visible-to-near-infrared irradiation at the stellate ganglion, not a conventional local PBM protocol, and its CRPS subgroup was very small. Two mouse publications report selected symptom improvements. A patient trial with a defined PBM dose, credible sham and validated pain and function measures is needed.

Publication and study types

  • Human1 small two-part report with a six-person CRPS subgroup
  • Animal2 (mouse; one directly categorized and one mapped from a nicotine-associated CRPS-I model)
  • No independent clinical PBM trial was identified.
  • The human report's blinded phase included healthy controls and should not be counted as a separate CRPS trial.
